In populations inhabiting the Iberian Peninsula, individuals typically attain total lengths of around 11.1 centimeters [Li = around 11.1 centimeters] at the end of their growth phase, a dimension that serves as the ultimate total length for this species under favorable conditions. The progression from a 0.0056 gram newborn to an 11.1 centimeter adult involves a series of molts and a substantial increase in tissue mass, reflecting the species’ capacity for rapid somatic development in productive environments. Field surveys in southern Portugal, for instance, have documented adults approaching this asymptotic length, confirming the relevance of these maximum size estimates for wild populations. Such measurements provide a critical baseline for comparing growth performance across the species’ expansive introduced range, which now spans four continents.

These thresholds mark the transition from the juvenile phase to the reproductively capable adult stage, after which individuals can participate in mating and egg production. Such latitudinal variation in reproductive frequency underscores the species’ remarkable plasticity in life-history scheduling, a trait that has undoubtedly facilitated its successful establishment across diverse climatic zones in Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
